title: And 40 divided by 20 is...
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton dissects a common modelling habit: a teacher working through simultaneous equations asks students trivial arithmetic questions such as 15x plus 5x or 40 divided by 20. These questions need no knowledge of the new process, and they do not reliably check that students are listening, yet they convince teacher and class that the explanation is landing. When students attempt the problem alone, they fail. Barton's alternatives are to assess prerequisites beforehand and deliver a clear explanation without questions, or to ask only listening checks about the new, vital step using techniques like Explain, Frame and Reframe. Real evidence of understanding then comes from a We Do on mini-whiteboards done step by step.
points: Easy questions during a worked example create an illusion of understanding for both teacher and students.
Such questions neither check the new process nor check that students are listening, since anyone can answer them after tuning in only when named.
Assess relevant prior knowledge first, then deliver a clear and concise explanation without interrupting questions.
If questions are asked during modelling, aim them at the new, vital part of the process and make them cognitively demanding.
Genuine evidence comes from the We Do completed on mini-whiteboards.
quotes: Mr L gives himself a metaphorical pat on the back, safe in knowing his students are following his work example. His students smile back, concluding they must understand what is happening because they are getting Mr L’s questions correct.
Are they to check students’ understanding of how to solve simultaneous questions? Definitely not, as zero knowledge of solving simultaneous equations is needed to answer them.
A student could have tuned out of the entire model, pricked up their ears as soon as their name was mentioned, and then answered the straightforward question they then heard.
They are there to convince everyone—teacher and student alike—that things are going well. Teachers convince themselves that their explanation makes sense as their students contribute to the solution.

Don’t ask any questions. Assess relevant prior knowledge first. Then deliver a clear and concise explanation linking the things that students are already familiar with within the novel process you are demonstrating.

And ask these questions for the new, vital part of the process, not the easy parts that anyone can get right without paying attention. Explain to students why you need to add these two equations, and then check if they can tell you.

Then, properly check for understanding by having students complete the We Do on mini-whiteboards using a Step-by-Step approach. Then, you will have real evidence of whether your explanation made sense.
